background.definition: Primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT) is the autonomous overproduction of parathyroid hormone (PTH), often causing hypercalcemia. Secondary hyperparathyroidism (SHPT) is the elevation of PTH as a physiologic response to hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, and/or decreased production of calcitriol (activated vitamin D) in the setting of chronic renal failure or malabsorption.

list.listitem: Twenty five new cases per 100,000 per year.
One to 4 persons per 1000 in the adult population.
Male-to-female ratio of 1:2.5.
PHPT is the most common cause of hypercalcemia in the outpatient setting.
PHPT is the underlying etiology for 90% of patients with hypercalcemia.
Eighty-five percent of PHPT caused by a single parathyroid adenoma.
Ten percent by hyperplasia of all parathyroid glands.
Four percent by double adenomas.
One percent by parathyroid carcinoma.
Hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia both stimulate PTH secretion.
Calcitriol (activated vitamin D) inhibits PTH production.
PTH stimulates bone resorption, leading to the release of calcium and phosphate.
PTH also acts on the kidneys to increase reabsorption of calcium and to inhibit phosphate reabsorption, thereby increasing serum calcium and decreasing serum phosphate.
In PHPT, the regulation of PTH levels by calcium, phosphate, and calcitriol is lost. Hypercalcemia results, as can hypophosphatemia and hypervitaminosis D.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Family history of multiple endocrine neoplasia syndromes (type 1 or 2)

Imaging is not required to make the diagnosis of PHPT, though it may be helpful in planning a parathyroidectomy. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Urine calcium-to-creatinine ratio less than 0.01 suggests FHH rather than PHPT, normal or high PTH
Elevated PTH-related peptide (PTHrP) with a low serum PTH, osteolytic metastases, or calcitriol-releasing tumor
Increased calcium intake, suppressed PTH levels
History of usage; calcium corrects once medication is withdrawn
Low serum vitamin D with a history of poor sun exposure or renal disease
Granulomatous disease (sarcoidosis, tuberculosis), or excess intake; will have a low PTH

list.listitem: The signs and symptoms of PHPT are caused by hypercalcemia and can manifest in multiple organ systems; they may be subtle and nonspecific. A large majority of patients with PHPT will be asymptomatic.
Past medical diagnoses related to hypercalcemia should raise suspicion of a secondary cause.
Neurologic and psychiatric: decreased cognitive function, depression, anxiety, fatigue, lethargy, and coma.
Cardiovascular: hypertension, shortened QT interval, cardiac arrhythmias, and vascular calcifications.
Gastrointestinal: constipation, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, pancreatitis, and peptic ulcer disease
Renal: renal insufficiency, renal tubular acidosis, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, nephrolithiasis, and nephrocalcinosis.
Musculoskeletal: muscle weakness, arthralgias, bone pain, osteoporosis, and osteitis fibrosa cystica.
Dermatologic: pruritus, keratitis, conjunctivitis, and calcification of the cornea.
Ultimately, PHPT is a diagnosis made by laboratory studies.
An increased serum calcium in the setting of inappropriately increased serum PTH levels has a sensitivity and specificity greater than 95% in diagnosing PHPT.

Total serum calcium concentration, corrected for the serum albumin concentration, should be used to measure hypercalcemia (for each 1 g/dL decrease in albumin from 4.0 g/dL the total serum calcium decreases by 0.8 mg/dL).
Alternatively, ionized serum calcium levels can be obtained.

Second-generation assays identify intact PTH and should be used to measure serum PTH; their sensitivity is 96%; first-generation PTH assays cross-react with PTH fragments and are insensitive for diagnostic purposes.
Parathyroid imaging is not necessary for the diagnosis of PHPT but can be helpful for parathyroidectomy planning.
Imaging either by technetium-labeled sestamibi uptake nuclear imaging (preferred), ultrasound, CT, or MRI can localize adenomas and ectopic glands.
A meta-analysis concluded that 4D-CT was more accurate than sestamibi-SPECT CT for localizing primary hyperparathyroidism.

Order serum calcium and albumin in patients with calcium-containing renal calculi, osteopenia, or osteoporosis, or if hyperparathyroidism is clinically suspected. Confirm hypercalcemia by calculating the corrected serum calcium level by the serum albumin level (for each 1 g/dL decrease in albumin from 4.0 g/dL the total serum calcium decreases by 0.8 mg/dL).
In patients with persistent hypercalcemia, order simultaneous measurements of serum calcium and PTH levels ().

If serum PTH is elevated, or inappropriately normal, the patient should have a 24-hour urine collection measuring urinary calcium and creatinine to rule out familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia. Hypophosphatemia and hyperchloremia may also be present but are not necessary for diagnosis.
Surgical excision of the problematic gland(s) is currently the only curative intervention for PHPT. C

Options for those not meeting surgical criteria, includes loop diuretics and possibly calcimimetic agents to maintain normocalcemia; bisphosphonates; avoidance of thiazide diuretics and lithium; adequate hydration and physical activity, and adequate calcium and vitamin D intake. C
There is no definitive long-term medical therapy for PHPT that has proved effective.
Patients should avoid thiazide diuretics and lithium. Loop diuretics can be used as second-line therapy to decrease calcium levels.

Bisphosphonates can improve bone mineral density but do not significantly change PTH levels. Estrogen replacement in postmenopausal women can stabilize or improve bone mineral density but does not significantly change PTH or calcium levels.

Calcimimetic agents, such as cinacalcet, can inhibit PTH secretion by increasing the sensitivity of calcium-sensing receptors of the parathyroid glands. Cinacalcet is approved for use in secondary hyperparathyroidism, and initial studies of its use in PHPT are promising in maintaining normal calcium levels and decreasing PTH levels.

Calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D), approved for treating secondary hyperparathyroidism, reduces PTH gene expression and parathyroid cell proliferation through the vitamin D receptor, which is also expressed in parathyroid cells.
Surgical excision of the problematic gland(s) is currently the only curative intervention for PHPT.

A practice guideline recommends parathyroidectomy for the following patients: all symptomatic patients and those who have experienced complications of PHPT; asymptomatic patients less than 50 years old; serum calcium level greater than 1.0 mg/dL above the normal limit; urinary calcium excretion greater than 400 mg/day; bone density at the lumbar, spine, hip, or distal radius 2.5 standard deviations below the peak bone mass; 30% decrease in renal function; patients unable to be followed-up appropriately.

A subsequent RCT randomized 191 adults with asymptomatic hyperparathyroidism to observation or surgery. After 2 years of follow-up, those who had surgery were more likely to have normal serum calcium levels but there were no improvements in quality of life compared with the observation only group.
Parathyroidectomy is successful at curing PHPT in 95% of patients when performed by an experienced parathyroid surgeon.
Complications rates of parathyroidectomy are low, but complications include recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, persistent/recurrent PHPT, and permanent hypoparathyroidism.
Surgical techniques have improved with preoperative imaging, intraoperative imaging, and intraoperative measurement of PTH to help verify successful resection.

A randomized trial compared F18-Choline PET/CT with MIBI SPECT/CT for the preoperative localization of parathyroid adenomas. After 1 month, more patients in the F18-Choline PET/CT group had normocalcemia (85% vs 56%, p = .03).

Patients with PHPT should maintain adequate calcium intake, as recommended for adults in the US, 1000 to 1200 mg/day. Patients should also maintain adequate vitamin D intake of 400 to 600 IU/day and stay well hydrated to reduce the risk of nephrolithiasis.
Physical activity can minimize bone resorption.
Secondary hyperparathyroidism (SHPT) is managed by adequate calcium intake, limited phosphorus intake, phosphate-binding medications, vitamin D analogs, calcimimetic agents, and hemodialysis.
A prospective cohort reported the results of microwave and radiofrequency ablation for 215 patients with SHPT. After therapy 85% achieved target PTH levels.

Tertiary hyperparathyroidism (resulting from prolonged SHPT) often requires parathyroidectomy because the parathyroid hyperplasia and elevated PTH are refractory to medical management (similar to PHPT).
Patients with hypercalcemic crisis or severe, symptomatic hypercalcemia should be hospitalized for immediate management.
Hypercalcemic crisis is a serious and potentially fatal complication of PHPT.
Hypercalcemia should be corrected with IV fluids, ideally normal saline.
Loop diuretics may be used to inhibit calcium reabsorption.
Bisphosphonates, calcitonin, and steroids have been shown to temporarily decrease serum calcium levels.
Urgent parathyroidectomy may be necessary in the setting of hypercalcemic crisis.
Parathyroidectomy by an experienced parathyroid surgeon is curative 95% of the time. B
Untreated patients should have twice yearly calcium levels drawn, yearly DEXA scan, and yearly renal function tests. C
Twenty-seven percent of asymptomatic PHPT patients will develop symptoms or other clinical indications for parathyroidectomy within 10 years. B
Twenty-seven percent of asymptomatic PHPT patients will develop symptoms or other clinical indications for parathyroidectomy within 10 years.
Untreated patients with worsening disease will experience progressive bone loss, leading to an increased risk of fracture.
Untreated patients will likely develop nephrolithiasis and gradual renal impairment.

A study involving reviewing medical records of 413 primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT) patients from January 2016 to April 2023, finding that 41.9% had renal stones and 48.6% required urological interventions.
Those with calcium levels above 13 mg/dL are at increased risk of premature death from hypercalcemic crisis.

From 1998 to 2005, 191 patients with mild primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT) were randomized to parathyroidectomy (PTX) vs observation without intervention. Over a follow-up period extending to 2018, mortality and morbidity rates, including cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events, cancer, fractures, and renal stones, were similar between the two groups, suggesting that parathyroidectomy does not reduce morbidity or mortality in mild PHPT.
Parathyroidectomy by an experienced surgeon is curative 95% of the time.
Symptoms of hypercalcemia resolve as calcium levels return to normal.
Bone mineral density improves with time as well.
Persistent hyperparathyroidism after parathyroidectomy suggests retained or ectopic parathyroid tissue.
In those patients not requiring surgery, or those in whom surgery is contraindicated or not advised, serum calcium should be measured every 6 months.
Patients should have yearly bone mass measurements of the lumbar spine, hip, and forearm.
Renal function should be monitored yearly by serum creatinine measurements.
Prevalence increases with age.
Elderly patients may have more subclinical and vague symptoms of hypercalcemia, such as fatigue, weakness, and bone pain.
The diagnosis and treatment of PHPT in elderly patients is often delayed compared with younger populations.
Maternal complications are the same as the adult population.
Fetal complications include intrauterine growth retardation, low birth weight, preterm delivery, intrauterine fetal demise, postpartum neonatal tetany, and permanent hypoparathyroidism.
Treatment is similar to that for the nonpregnant patient, and surgery should be performed after the first trimester, if possible.
If medical management is pursued, perform frequent fetal surveillance with level II ultrasound, growth scans, amniotic fluid indices, and nonstress testing starting at 28 to 32 weeks.
Diagnosis is often delayed, and pediatric patients are more often symptomatic with more severe end-organ damage than adults.
A larger proportion of PHPT is due to Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndromes (MEN) and familial hyperparathyroidism in the pediatric population compared with adults.
Parathyroidectomy is the treatment of choice.
